triage.name: Tinea Infections
triage.reason: Common dermatophyte infection with classic rash patterns; diagnosis is made by history and exam with KOH confirmation, and mimics eczema and psoriasis.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'fungal culture of skin, hair, or nail' was in ['confirmatory', 'supporting'], kept ['confirmatory']

demographics: Tinea capitis is most common in children, especially those of African descent
Tinea pedis and tinea cruris are more common in adolescent and adult males
Tinea corporis occurs at any age
Onychomycosis is more common in older adults

risk_factors.text: Close contact with an infected person or animal (especially kittens, puppies, rodents)
Walking barefoot on damp communal surfaces (shower floors, locker rooms, pool decks)
Sharing combs, hats, towels, or clothing
Warm, humid climate or excessive sweating
Tight, non-breathable clothing or occlusive footwear
Household member with a dermatophyte infection

comorbidities: Atopic dermatitis (predisposes to skin barrier disruption)
social_history: Use of communal showers or locker rooms
Pet ownership (especially young cats or dogs)
exposures: Infected household member or close contact
risk_medications: Topical corticosteroids (can mask or worsen tinea)

chief_complaints.text: There's a red ring on my skin
The skin between my toes is itchy and peeling
My groin is itchy and burning
I have a bald spot on my head
My toenails are thick and discolored

hpi.progression: Slowly enlarges; may spread to other body sites or to close contacts
hpi.location: Depends on type: tinea corporis on trunk or limbs; tinea pedis between toes or on soles; tinea cruris in groin; tinea capitis on scalp; onychomycosis on nails
hpi.quality: Itchy, sometimes burning; rash may be scaly or ring-shaped
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; usually not severe but can be very uncomfortable
hpi.timing: Constant; itching may be worse at night or after sweating

associated_symptoms.text: Cracked or peeling skin between toes
Secondary bacterial infection with pus or pain

pertinent_negatives: Travel to areas with endemic fungal disease

argues_against: Well-demarcated silvery plaques on extensor surfaces (psoriasis)
Vesicles in a dermatomal distribution (herpes zoster)

atypical.how_it_differs: Tinea capitis is common and presents with scaly patches and broken hairs rather than a classic ring; may have little itching.
Onychomycosis and tinea pedis are more common; skin may be dry and fissured rather than inflamed.
Lesions can be extensive, atypical, and deeper, sometimes with nodules or abscesses.
Tinea pedis is more severe and often complicated by bacterial infection; nails frequently involved.

general.moderate: Well-appearing but scratching or visibly uncomfortable
general.severe: Ill-appearing with extensive or inflamed lesions; may be uncomfortable but not toxic
general.critical: Not applicable; tinea is not a critical illness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the trunk and limbs in good lighting
findings.finding: Annular, erythematous, scaly plaque with an active raised border and central clearing

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the affected skin
findings.finding: Scaly, flaky patches with a rough surface

findings.maneuver: Inspect the web spaces between the toes
findings.finding: Maceration, scaling, fissuring, or peeling between the toes, especially the fourth and fifth web spaces

findings.maneuver: Inspect the soles and plantar surfaces
findings.finding: Diffuse dry scaling, erythema, or a moccasin-like distribution on the sole

findings.maneuver: Inspect the inguinal folds and upper inner thighs
findings.finding: Erythematous, scaly plaque with an active advancing border in the groin, often with central clearing; scrotum usually spared

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scalp with a bright light and part the hair
findings.finding: Scaly, erythematous patches on the scalp with broken hairs or black dots at the follicular openings

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scalp for areas of hair loss
findings.finding: Patchy hair loss with broken hairs, not completely smooth bald skin
Thickened, discolored (yellow-brown), crumbling nails with subungual debris; may have onycholysis

findings.maneuver: Palpate the cervical, occipital, and inguinal lymph nodes
findings.finding: Regional lymphadenopathy, especially with tinea capitis or secondary bacterial infection

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and lips
Inspect the rash for vesicles or bullae
Inspect the rash for pustules or purulent drainage
Inspect the elbows, knees, and extensor surfaces
findings.finding: No well-demarcated silvery plaques on extensor surfaces

findings.maneuver: Inspect the rash distribution and ask about pain
findings.finding: No vesicular rash in a single dermatomal distribution

initial.why: First-line bedside test: scrapings from the active border show branching septate hyphae, confirming a dermatophyte
Helps screen tinea capitis; some dermatophytes fluoresce blue-green

confirmatory.test: Fungal culture of skin, hair, or nail
confirmatory.why: Definitive identification of the dermatophyte species when KOH is negative or treatment has failed

supporting.why: Shows characteristic features such as comma hairs and corkscrew hairs in tinea capitis

not_indicated.why: Tinea is a superficial infection; blood counts are normal and do not change management
Inflammatory markers are not useful for a superficial dermatophyte infection
Not useful for diagnosing or managing tinea
Reserved for atypical or refractory lesions where the diagnosis is unclear; not routine

decision_points: Confirm the diagnosis with KOH before starting systemic therapy
Scalp or nail involvement requires oral therapy because topical agents do not penetrate hair follicles or nail plate
Consider bacterial superinfection if there is pain, purulence, or marked erythema

differential.name: Nummular eczema
differential.why_considered: Coin-shaped, scaly, itchy patches on the limbs that can look like tinea corporis

history: Personal or family history of atopic dermatitis, asthma, or allergic rhinitis
Dry skin, worse in winter
No known contact with infected person or animal
exam: Multiple symmetric round patches without central clearing
No active raised advancing border
Lesions often on extensor surfaces and trunk

differential.name: Psoriasis
differential.why_considered: Well-demarcated, scaly, erythematous plaques that can be mistaken for tinea corporis

history: Chronic, recurring plaques that may wax and wane
Family history of psoriasis
Nail pitting or joint pain
exam: Silvery scale on well-demarcated plaques, often on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees) and scalp
Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed)
No central clearing
imaging: Skin biopsy shows epidermal hyperplasia with parakeratosis and Munro microabscesses if performed

differential.name: Contact dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Itchy, red, scaly rash that can appear on exposed skin and mimic tinea

history: Onset after contact with a new soap, cosmetic, metal, or plant
Burning or itching at the site of contact
Improves when the offending agent is avoided
exam: Erythema, edema, vesicles, or weeping in the acute phase; lichenification in chronic phase
Distribution matches the area of contact, often with sharp borders
No central clearing or active border
labs: Patch testing may identify the allergen

differential.name: Pityriasis rosea
differential.why_considered: Scaly, oval, pink patches on the trunk that can resemble tinea corporis

history: Often begins with a single larger herald patch followed by a generalized eruption
Mild itching, sometimes preceding viral-like symptoms
Self-limited, resolves in 6–8 weeks
exam: Oval patches with a collarette of scale, distributed along skin cleavage lines (Christmas tree pattern) on the trunk
No active advancing border or central clearing

differential.name: Erythrasma
differential.why_considered: Brown, scaly patches in the groin or between toes that can be mistaken for tinea cruris or tinea pedis

history: Often asymptomatic or mildly itchy
More common in warm, humid climates and in people with diabetes
No response to antifungal therapy
exam: Well-demarcated, brown, slightly scaly patches in intertriginous areas
Wood lamp examination shows coral-red fluorescence
labs: Bacterial culture may grow Corynebacterium minutissimum

differential.name: Cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Tinea pedis can be complicated by bacterial cellulitis, and both cause leg redness and swelling
differential.trigger: Pain, warmth, swelling, fever, or rapidly spreading erythema in a patient with tinea pedis

history: Acute onset of pain, warmth, and swelling
Fever and chills
Often follows a break in the skin such as tinea pedis or a wound
exam: Unilateral, ill-defined, warm, tender erythema
Lymphangitic streaking or regional lymphadenopathy
Systemic signs such as fever and tachycardia
labs: Leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR)
Blood cultures may be positive in severe cases
imaging: Ultrasound or MRI if abscess or deep infection is suspected

differential.name: Lyme disease (erythema migrans)
differential.why_considered: Expanding annular rash that can be mistaken for tinea corporis
differential.trigger: Recent tick bite or exposure in an endemic area, with an expanding ring-like rash

history: Recent tick bite or travel to an endemic area
Rash expands over days to weeks
May have fever, headache, myalgias, or arthralgias
exam: Single expanding erythematous ring with central clearing (targetoid) at the site of the bite
No scale or active scaly border
May have facial palsy or joint swelling in later stages
labs: Serology for Borrelia burgdorferi (ELISA with Western blot confirmation) may be positive

differential.name: Seborrheic dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Scaly, itchy scalp and facial rash that can resemble tinea capitis or tinea faciei

history: Chronic, recurring rash with flaking
Often worse in winter or with stress
No hair loss or broken hairs
exam: Greasy, yellowish scales on erythematous skin, often on scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and chest
No annular lesions or active border
Hair remains intact

severity.mild: Localized, small area of involvement; mild itching; no secondary infection; responds to topical antifungals
severity.moderate: More extensive or multiple sites; significant itching or discomfort; may require oral therapy for scalp or nail involvement
severity.severe: Widespread, inflamed, or secondarily infected lesions; marked discomfort; requires systemic therapy and possibly antibiotics for bacterial superinfection
severity.critical: Not applicable; tinea is not a life-threatening condition

red_flags.finding: Rapidly spreading erythema, warmth, pain, fever, or purulent drainage
red_flags.meaning: Suggests bacterial cellulitis or superinfection, which requires prompt antibiotic treatment

red_flags.finding: Pain out of proportion to exam or systemic toxicity
red_flags.meaning: May indicate deeper infection such as abscess or necrotizing fasciitis, especially in immunocompromised patients

red_flags.finding: Scalp involvement with broken hairs, black dots, or significant alopecia
red_flags.meaning: Tinea capitis requires oral therapy and can be contagious; topical therapy alone is ineffective

red_flags.finding: Nail involvement with thickening, discoloration, or crumbling
red_flags.meaning: Onychomycosis requires prolonged oral therapy and can be a source of reinfection

red_flags.finding: Immunocompromised state with extensive or atypical lesions
red_flags.meaning: Higher risk of deeper invasion and atypical presentation; may need systemic therapy and specialist referral

complications.name: Secondary bacterial infection (cellulitis, impetigo)
clues: Increasing pain, warmth, swelling, or purulent drainage

complications.name: Kerion (inflammatory tinea capitis)
clues: Boggy, tender, pus-filled mass on the scalp
May lead to scarring alopecia if untreated

complications.name: Scarring alopecia
clues: Permanent hair loss after severe or untreated tinea capitis

complications.name: Onychomycosis with nail destruction
clues: May cause pain or difficulty walking

complications.name: Dermatophytid (id) reaction
clues: Vesicular or eczematous eruption on hands or other distant sites
Occurs in response to a dermatophyte infection elsewhere
Resolves with treatment of the primary infection

special_populations.differences: Tinea capitis is common and often presents with scaly patches, broken hairs, and little itching; requires oral therapy. Kerion may occur.
Onychomycosis and tinea pedis are more common; skin may be dry and fissured; increased risk of bacterial superinfection and lower extremity cellulitis.
Lesions can be extensive, atypical, and deeper; may require systemic therapy and have a higher risk of complications.
Tinea pedis is more severe and often complicated by bacterial infection; nails frequently involved; increased risk of foot ulcers and cellulitis.
Topical antifungals are generally safe; oral azoles should be avoided in the first trimester and used with caution thereafter; consult with obstetric provider.

key_questions.question: Where on your body did the rash start, and where is it now?
key_questions.looking_for: Site determines the type: trunk or limbs (corporis), between toes or soles (pedis), groin (cruris), scalp (capitis), nails (onychomycosis)

key_questions.question: What does the rash look like — is it a ring with clear skin in the middle, or a solid scaly patch?
key_questions.looking_for: Annular lesion with an active raised border and central clearing suggests tinea corporis

key_questions.question: How long has it been there, and is it getting bigger or spreading?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over days to weeks with slow enlargement; helps distinguish from acute eruptions

key_questions.question: Does it itch or burn? What makes it worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Itching worse with heat, sweating, tight clothing, or occlusive footwear

key_questions.question: Have you been around anyone else with a similar rash, or a pet with patches of hair loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Contact with an infected person or animal (especially kittens, puppies, rodents) supports dermatophyte transmission

key_questions.question: Do you walk barefoot in shared showers, locker rooms, or around a pool?
key_questions.looking_for: Exposure to damp communal surfaces, a classic risk factor for tinea pedis

key_questions.question: Do you share combs, hats, towels, or clothing with anyone?
key_questions.looking_for: Shared personal items, especially relevant for tinea capitis in children

key_questions.question: Have you tried any creams on it, especially steroid creams?
key_questions.looking_for: Topical corticosteroids can mask or worsen tinea (tinea incognito); prior antifungal use may partially suppress it

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, HIV, or take any medicines that suppress your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression or diabetes predisposes to more extensive, atypical, or complicated infection

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, chills, or increasing pain, warmth, or swelling in the area?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests bacterial cellulitis or superinfection requiring prompt antibiotic treatment

key_questions.question: Is there any pus, drainage, or a boggy tender lump on your scalp?
key_questions.looking_for: Purulence suggests secondary bacterial infection; a boggy scalp mass suggests kerion

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any hair loss, broken hairs, or bald spots?
key_questions.looking_for: Patchy alopecia with broken hairs suggests tinea capitis, which requires oral therapy

key_questions.question: Are your nails thick, discolored, or crumbling?
key_questions.looking_for: Onychomycosis, which requires prolonged oral therapy and can be a source of reinfection

key_questions.question: Do you have a personal or family history of eczema, asthma, or psoriasis?
key_questions.looking_for: Atopic or psoriatic history raises alternative diagnoses such as nummular eczema or psoriasis

reasoning_points: Itchy, scaly rash with an annular active border and central clearing, or maceration between the toes, or an inguinal plaque with scrotal sparing
Gradual onset over days to weeks with slow enlargement, rather than an acute eruption
Risk exposure: contact with an infected person or pet, damp communal surfaces, or shared personal items
Absence of systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats
No new medication or recent antibiotic exposure to suggest a drug eruption
KOH microscopy of scrapings from the active border showing branching septate hyphae confirms the diagnosis
Scalp or nail involvement requires oral therapy because topical agents do not penetrate hair follicles or the nail plate
Consider bacterial superinfection when there is pain, warmth, purulence, or fever

easy: Classic annular plaque with an active raised border and central clearing on the trunk or limb
Itchy rash in a patient who walks barefoot in locker rooms or shares a home with an infected pet
No systemic symptoms and no new medications
medium: Tinea pedis presenting as dry, fissured skin between the toes without a classic ring
Tinea cruris with an inguinal plaque and scrotal sparing, mimicking erythrasma or candidal intertrigo
Tinea capitis in a child with scaly patches and broken hairs but little itching
Partial improvement from an over-the-counter antifungal cream, obscuring the classic appearance
hard: Tinea incognito: atypical, poorly demarcated rash after topical corticosteroid use
Onychomycosis with thickened, crumbling nails and no skin findings
Immunocompromised patient with extensive or deeper lesions, nodules, or abscesses
Tinea pedis complicated by bacterial cellulitis with fever, warmth, and spreading erythema
Annular rash that is actually erythema migrans from Lyme disease or nummular eczema
